tip: Name your variables for what they represent, not what they hold. `userAge` beats `data` every time.
Commit often with meaningful messages. `git commit -m 'fix'` is a crime. Describe the *why*, not just the *what*.
Avoid `any`. Use `unknown` instead and narrow the type explicitly — your future self will thank you.
Don't optimize prematurely. Profile first, then optimize the actual bottleneck — not what you *think* is slow.
Keep components small and focused. If a component does more than one thing, it should probably be two components.
Design your API endpoints around resources and actions, not implementation details. REST is a mindset, not just a convention.
Never store secrets in your code or `.env` files committed to git. Use a secrets manager or environment injection at runtime.
Use CSS custom properties (variables) for your design tokens. Consistent spacing and color is the hallmark of a polished UI.
When stuck on a bug, explain it to someone — or a rubber duck. Articulating the problem often reveals the solution.
Design for failure. Assume any external service will go down. Build retries, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation from day one.
When prompting LLMs, be specific about the output format. JSON output with a schema example is more reliable than freeform text.
Test behavior, not implementation. Tests that break on every refactor aren't protecting you — they're slowing you down.
The Pomodoro technique works. 25 minutes of deep focus, 5-minute break, repeat. Your brain is not a computer — it needs rest cycles.
Read the source. When documentation is unclear, the code is the ground truth. Don't be afraid to dive in.
Always index columns you `WHERE`, `JOIN`, or `ORDER BY`. Unindexed queries on large tables will kill your app's performance.
Never block the event loop. Move heavy computation to worker threads or background queues — keep your API responsive.
Lift state only as high as it needs to go. Global state managers are powerful tools; don't reach for them when local state works.
Automate your deployment pipeline from day one. Manual deployments are where bugs hide and confidence dies.
Code reviews are for knowledge sharing, not gatekeeping. Ask questions, suggest improvements, and always assume good intent.
Separate your concerns. A function that fetches data, transforms it, AND renders UI is three functions pretending to be one.
Chain-of-thought prompting dramatically improves LLM reasoning on complex tasks. Ask the model to 'think step by step'.
Master `flexbox` and `CSS grid`. They replace 90% of layout hacks. If you're fighting CSS, you're probably not using these enough.
Use `const` by default, `let` when you need to reassign. Avoid `var` entirely — its function scope causes subtle, hard-to-find bugs.
The best UX is invisible. If users notice your UI, it means something confused them. Clarity > cleverness.
Prefer `async/await` over raw `.then()` chains. It reads like synchronous code and makes error handling with `try/catch` natural.
Write docs as if your future self needs to understand this code in 6 months at 2am before a production incident. Be kind.
The boy scout rule: always leave the code cleaner than you found it. Small, consistent improvements compound over time.
Cache at the right layer: browser, CDN, server, or database. Cache invalidation is hard — only cache what you control.
Never swallow errors silently. Log them, alert on them, and handle them gracefully. Silent failures are the hardest bugs to find.
Use Firestore security rules as your first line of defense. Never trust the client — validate everything server-side or with rules.
